scenes.tts: A liver cell and a kidney cell carry the same genome. Yet each one reads a different set of genes, and its daughters keep reading the same set. Eukaryotic DNA is packed into chromatin, and packed DNA is hard to read. How does a cell choose? Part of the answer is a stretch of DNA called an enhancer.
scenes.visual: Two cells, one genome strip with genes marked by question marks; a liver cell and a kidney cell each light up a different set of genes, then a stretch of DNA beside one gene is ringed and named enhancer.
scenes.narration: A liver cell and a kidney cell carry the same genome. Yet each one reads a different set of genes, and its daughters keep reading the same set. Eukaryotic DNA is packed into chromatin, and packed DNA is hard to read. How does a cell choose? Part of the answer is a stretch of DNA called an enhancer.

scenes.tts: An enhancer is DNA that raises transcription from a promoter, at a distance and in either orientation. Transcription factors bind it and recruit coactivators and the Mediator complex. Mediator bridges the enhancer to R N A polymerase two while the DNA between them loops out. To map one, scientists clone a region beside a promoter that drives luciferase, a reporter. This region of six hundred base pairs holds three elements: A, B, and C.
scenes.visual: An enhancer far from a promoter, factors on it, Mediator bridging with the DNA looped out; then a cloned 600 bp bar split into A, B, C beside a promoter and a luciferase reporter box.
scenes.caption: An enhancer is DNA that raises transcription from a promoter, at a distance and in either orientation. Transcription factors bind it and recruit coactivators and the Mediator complex. Mediator bridges the enhancer to RNA polymerase II while the DNA between them loops out. To map one, scientists clone a region beside a promoter that drives luciferase, a reporter. This region of 600 base pairs holds three elements: A, B, and C.

scenes.tts: First, delete each element in turn and test liver cells, with each value a mean of repeats. Activity is scaled so the promoter alone scores one. The full region scores one hundred. Delete A, and it still scores ninety-five, so A is dispensable. Delete B, and it falls to four; delete C, and it falls to thirty.
scenes.visual: Four constructs in turn, each with a bar growing to its liver score: 100, 95, 4, 30.

scenes.tts: Now test the pieces alone. B alone scores five, so B is not sufficient. C alone scores two. B and C together score ninety. If their effects added, you would expect about six; if they multiplied, about ten. Ninety is about nine times the multiplied guess, so B and C work together.
scenes.visual: B alone and C alone as short bars, then B plus C as a tall bar; the added and multiplied guesses as tick marks far below it.
scenes.caption: Now test the pieces alone. B alone scores 5, so B is not sufficient. C alone scores 2. B and C together score 90. If their effects added, you would expect about 6; if they multiplied, about 10. 90 is about nine times the multiplied guess, so B and C work together.

scenes.tts: Reverse B and C, and it still scores eighty-eight, so orientation does not matter here. Now try kidney cells, where nothing scores above two. The simplest reading is that kidney cells lack a factor that B or C needs. A kidney repressor would also fit.
scenes.visual: B plus C flipped end to end gives a bar of 88; then the kidney column, every bar at or below 2, with two possible readings.

scenes.tts: So the minimal liver enhancer is B plus C. This fits factors on both pieces that must be present at once, like a committee that needs the right members. That is combinatorial control. But this is a reporter test. Its role at the native gene needs a test there, such as deleting B in the genome.
scenes.visual: B and C each with a factor, the reporter lighting only when both are present; then a native chromosome with B deleted as the next test.
